what_it_does: Scientific simulations, graph algorithms, and database workloads constantly need to read data at addresses that are themselves stored in memory — a pattern like 'read A at the location given by B[i]' — and this scrambled access pattern wastes most of the memory chip's available bandwidth because the accesses land on random rows and columns in no useful order. DX100 is a programmable hardware accelerator that sits between processor cores and memory, collects a large batch of these indirect addresses, reorders them to minimize wasted memory chip transitions, and fires them off in an order that nearly saturates the available bandwidth, achieving 2.6x speedup over a multicore baseline.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Main memory (DRAM chips) is organized in rows. Opening a row to read from it takes time; reading multiple values from the same open row is fast. Ordinary processor cores can only keep 32–128 memory requests in flight at once, so they can reorder only within that tiny window — too small to fix scattered indirect access patterns. DX100 expands that window to 16,000 requests at a time.

How it works. The CPU offloads a whole tile of indirect work to DX100 with a small 8-instruction set (load, store, read-modify-write, stream, arithmetic, and range-loop fusion). DX100 first uses a streaming unit to pull the index array (the B[i] values) into a local scratchpad — a fast private buffer. Then the Indirect Access unit reads those indices and maps each one to its physical row and column in the memory chips. It stores this information in a Row Table (a lookup structure that groups indices by which memory row they will land in) and a Word Table (a linked list that tracks multiple accesses to the same column). Once a full tile of indices is sorted into this structure, the Request Generator scans rows in order and fires requests to the memory controller interleaved across different memory channels and bank groups, hitting the same open row consecutively before moving on.

The key design choice. DX100 bypasses the CPU's cache hierarchy entirely for indirect accesses (which almost always miss the cache anyway), injecting requests directly into the memory controller. A small coherency agent snoops the directory to avoid stale data, so correctness is maintained without the overhead of cache-coherent routing. A compiler built on MLIR automatically detects and transforms indirect loops in existing code, covering over 99% of graph workload accesses automatically.

The result. On 12 benchmarks from scientific computing, graph analytics, and database workloads, DX100 achieves 2.6x speedup over a 4-core baseline and 2.0x over the best existing indirect prefetcher. Memory bandwidth utilization improves 3.9x on average, and DRAM row-buffer hit rate increases 2.7x.
